author: A Robot
objectives: Represent a two-dimensional vector by its magnitude and direction, and equivalently by its horizontal and vertical components.
Add vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method to identify the resultant.
Decompose a vector into components along x- and y-axes and reconstruct the original vector.
Explain why horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent under gravity.
Describe projectile motion component-wise (horizontal constant, vertical accelerating) and identify maximum height when vertical velocity is zero.
Predict and test how launch angle and speed affect range and maximum height; identify the 45° condition for maximum range at fixed speed on level ground.

modules.description: Introduce a single draggable 3D vector with live-updating magnitude and direction readouts relative to visible axes.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Interpret a vector as a quantity with both magnitude and direction.
Relate the vector’s length and orientation to numerical magnitude and angle indicators.
instructions: Grab the vector arrowhead.
Drag the arrowhead to re-orient the vector.
Observe how magnitude and direction labels update in real time.

clips.changeMeaning: Axis guides and the vector with its magnitude/direction labels appear, establishing a clear reference for subsequent vector manipulations.
clips.narration: Vectors represent quantities with both magnitude and direction. A vector is fully described only when you specify how long it is and where it points.

clips.changeMeaning: The arrow is made interactive for dragging; labels are intended to update live while keeping sparse scene changes.
clips.narration: Drag the arrowhead. Notice how the magnitude and direction readouts update to match the vector’s orientation.

clips.changeMeaning: The vector pose is held stable while the student changes viewpoint, emphasizing that the vector itself is unchanged.
clips.narration: Rotate your viewpoint around the vector. The geometry stays fixed; only your perceived angles change.

modules.description: Show two draggable vectors (blue and green) laid tip-to-tail and compute a resultant (red) that updates continuously and supports commutativity verification.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Add vectors graphically using the tip-to-tail method.
Identify the resultant as the vector from the first tail to the final head.
Verify commutativity by swapping order.
instructions: Grab and re-orient the blue or green vector.
Watch the red resultant anchored at the origin.
Swap the order of adding (toggle) and compare.

clips.changeMeaning: The instructional text cues the geometric construction so students know exactly how to position the second arrow.
clips.narration: To add vectors, lay them tip-to-tail. The resultant runs from the origin tail to the final head.

clips.changeMeaning: A sparse update anchors the resultant conceptually; it is intended to remain consistent with the student’s current blue/green orientations.
clips.narration: Reorient the vectors. The red resultant updates continuously as the tip-to-tail geometry changes.

clips.changeMeaning: Swapping the addition order triggers the alternate construction and lets students compare resultant direction and location.
clips.narration: Now swap the order: lay green on top of blue. The resultant ends up in the same direction and location.

modules.description: Break a single vector into axis-aligned component arrows that reconstruct the original as they are resized.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Decompose a vector into x and y components along chosen axes.
Interpret decomposition as reversed addition: components add tip-to-tail to reproduce the original vector.
instructions: Grab and resize the component arrows.
Observe how the original vector reconstructs as the component sum changes.

clips.changeMeaning: The original vector and the two main planar component arrows appear, with a right-triangle visual hint activated for 2D geometry.
clips.narration: Decomposition breaks a vector into components along chosen axes. It’s reversed addition: the components add tip-to-tail to reproduce the original.

clips.changeMeaning: Sparse updates enable pointer control so students can resize the component lengths while the original vector reconstructs via their sum.
clips.narration: Grab and resize each component arrow. As you change them, the original vector reconstructs from their tip-to-tail sum.

clips.changeMeaning: The label is updated to explicitly connect component lengths and vector magnitude through right-triangle intuition used later for projectiles.
clips.narration: For motion in a plane, x and y form right-triangle legs. The vector magnitude connects to those legs through right-triangle relationships.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Transition to Projectile Motion Plane
modules.description: Switch to a 2D vertical plane with labeled horizontal and vertical axes, showing a projectile ball and an initial velocity vector.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Represent projectile motion in a vertical analysis plane using x (horizontal) and y (vertical).
Justify component independence by noting gravity acts only vertically.
instructions: Observe the axes labels on the plane.
Relate the initial velocity arrow’s angle to its x and y components.

clips.changeMeaning: The projectile analysis plane appears and the projectile + initial velocity arrow are placed at the launch point.
clips.narration: Now we apply vector tools to projectile motion in a vertical plane. The motion is genuinely two-dimensional even though the world is three-dimensional.

clips.changeMeaning: The plane label is updated to emphasize that gravity affects only the vertical component, motivating independence of x and y motion.
clips.narration: Gravity accelerates only in the vertical direction, so the horizontal component can be treated as constant.

clips.changeMeaning: The initial velocity arrow’s orientation is held steady to help students focus on how the launch angle sets x/y components.
clips.narration: The launch angle tells you how the initial velocity splits into horizontal and vertical components.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5 — Projectile Motion with Component Arrows
modules.description: Launch a projectile and show live horizontal and vertical component arrows updating over time while the ball follows a parabolic path.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Interpret the horizontal component as constant during flight.
Interpret the vertical component as changing under gravity, vanishing at maximum height.
Explain the parabolic trajectory as combined independent x and y motions.
instructions: Launch the projectile.
Watch the horizontal arrow keep the same length and the vertical arrow shrink to zero at the peak.
Switch view mode if available.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables the trajectory trail and both component arrows so the subsequent launch can be interpreted as independent x and y motions.
clips.narration: We’ll split the initial velocity into horizontal (constant) and vertical (gravity-affected) components.

clips.changeMeaning: During the flight, the horizontal component scale is held fixed (constant), while the vertical component is updated sparsely to represent changing magnitude over time.
clips.narration: Launch and watch closely: the horizontal component stays the same length, while the vertical component changes as the ball moves up and down.

clips.changeMeaning: At peak height the vertical component is set to zero length, visually marking the moment when vertical velocity becomes zero.
clips.narration: At maximum height, the vertical velocity is zero. That’s when the vertical component arrow has zero length.

clips.changeMeaning: Overhead mode changes the visual interpretation to emphasize the uniform horizontal progression when viewing the same trajectory.
clips.narration: Try overhead view to see the horizontal progression more directly.

modules.description: Provide launch controls for repeated trials. Display range and keep a history panel so students identify the angle that maximizes range at fixed speed.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Test how launch angle affects projectile range at fixed speed.
Identify the maximum-range condition at 45° for equal launch/landing height.
Relate the result to equal horizontal and vertical component magnitudes at launch.
instructions: Set a launch speed and try different angles.
After each launch, record the range.
Look for the largest range and then test complementary angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables the history and range readout so each launch attempt can be compared side-by-side.
clips.narration: Set a fixed launch speed, then try different launch angles. After each launch, record the displayed range.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds two sample history entries showing complementary angles yield the same range on level ground for fixed speed.
clips.narration: Notice the symmetry: angles symmetric about 45°, like 30° and 60°, give the same range for the same speed.

clips.changeMeaning: The range readout is updated to explicitly confirm the discovered maximum-range condition at 45°.
clips.narration: For any fixed launch speed, the range is maximized at about 45° on level ground.

clips.changeMeaning: Sparsely sets both component arrow scales equal to visually represent the ‘equal components’ condition at 45°.
clips.narration: At 45°, the horizontal and vertical component magnitudes match. That balance produces the maximum range.

modules.description: Targeting task: set launch angle and speed to hit a fixed ground target. Each successful hit advances to the next target distance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply projectile motion reasoning to hit a target at fixed height.
Recognize typical existence of two complementary launch angles for the same target distance.
Transfer decomposition intuition into a practical prediction task.
instructions: Hit the red target by selecting launch angle and speed.
Try a complementary angle pair for at least one target (optional).
When you hit, proceed to the next target.

clips.changeMeaning: Spawns the first target, enables feedback and trajectory trail, and reminds students about the two-solution pattern.
clips.narration: Your mission: choose launch angle and speed so the projectile lands on the target. For many distances, two different angles can work.

clips.changeMeaning: Updates feedback text to a checking state for a sparse success detection loop.
clips.narration: Launch and watch where it lands. When you hit, feedback will confirm success and advance you.

clips.changeMeaning: Sparse update moves the target farther away at the same elevation and prompts a new attempt.
clips.narration: Next target. Use the same component reasoning to reach the new distance.

clips.changeMeaning: Reinforces the complementary-angle strategy at the end of the challenge for consolidation.
clips.narration: Remember: once you find one solution angle, its complement often yields the same range. Try it if you want.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Free Exploration Sandbox & Recap Prompt
modules.description: Sandbox: adjust launch angle, speed, initial height, and gravity strength (0 to 5g). Live component arrows and trajectory trail remain visible.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Investigate how gravity strength and initial height affect flight and range.
Explore limiting cases (0g, strong gravity).
Consolidate independence of x and y motion under varying g.
instructions: Try halving gravity and compare range.
Try 5g and observe the change.
Launch from a ~50 m platform and test whether 45° is still optimal.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables the trajectory trail and gravity indicator and provides guiding questions for exploration.
clips.narration: Free exploration time. Adjust launch angle, speed, initial height, and gravity strength while watching the component arrows.

clips.changeMeaning: Sets gravity to zero and uses a sparse scale cue to show vertical component behavior without parabolic curvature.
clips.narration: If gravity is zero, vertical velocity doesn’t accelerate. The trajectory becomes a straight line in the x-y plane.

clips.changeMeaning: Increases gravity to 5g and sparsely reduces the vertical component arrow size to indicate faster vertical change and shorter flight.
clips.narration: With 5g, vertical motion changes much faster. Expect a shorter flight and a different range than on Earth gravity.

clips.changeMeaning: Focuses the prompt on the high-platform scenario, preparing students to test whether the 45° rule generalizes.
clips.narration: From a high platform, the assumptions behind the 45° result can change. Test it—does the optimal angle shift?

modules.description: Recap the conceptual sequence with a concept board and highlighted markers.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall key stages: magnitude/direction, addition, decomposition, projectile application, independence, and 45° maximum range.
Integrate how component reasoning explains trajectory features.
instructions: Watch the recap highlights.
Mentally link each highlight to the corresponding scene.

clips.changeMeaning: The recap board appears and highlights the first concept (vectors as magnitude and direction).
clips.narration: Let’s connect the full story: we started with vectors, then used addition and decomposition.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights advance to vector addition and decomposition, connecting each concept stage visually.
clips.narration: Tip-to-tail addition gives the resultant. Decomposition is reversed addition: components add back to the original vector.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights focus on applying component reasoning to projectile motion and the independence of horizontal and vertical motion.
clips.narration: For projectiles, horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity accelerates under gravity. Together they produce the parabolic path.

clips.changeMeaning: The final marker emphasizes the 45° maximum-range result to complete the conceptual chain.
clips.narration: Finally, on level ground with fixed launch speed, maximum range occurs at 45°. That’s when the initial horizontal and vertical components balance.
